extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS 2014 reviewers, Area Chairs, and program committee members (conference paper reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Reviewer instructions and scoring rubric for NeurIPS 2014 conference submissions, covering quantitative scores (1–10), impact and confidence scores, qualitative criteria (quality, clarity, originality, significance), reviewer workload limits, and calibration guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Evaluation (1–10 score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give a paper score of between 1 and 10 for each paper. The program committee will interpret the numerical score in the following way: 10 Top 5% of accepted NeurIPS papers, a seminal paper for the ages. I will consider not reviewing for NeurIPS again if this is rejected. 9 Top 15% of accepted NeurIPS papers, an excellent paper, a strong accept. I will fight for acceptance. 8 Top 50% of accepted NeurIPS papers, a very good paper, a clear accept. I vote and argue for acceptance. 7 Good paper, accept. I vote for acceptance, although would not be upset if it were rejected. 6 Marginally above the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for accepting it, but leaving it out of the program would be no great loss. 5 Marginally below the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for rejecting it, but having it in the program would not be that bad. 4 An OK paper, but not good enough. A rejection. I vote for rejecting it, although would not be upset if it were accepted. 3 A clear rejection. I vote and argue for rejection. 2 A strong rejection. I’m surprised it was submitted to this conference. I will fight for rejection. 1 Trivial or wrong or known. I’m surprised anybody wrote such a paper. I will consider not reviewing for NeurIPS again if this is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper; reviewers should NOT assume they have an unbiased sample nor should they adjust scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. Use the mapping above to communicate relative strength; free-text comments should support the numeric score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Score (2/1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of the Quality Score, identify papers that are very different, original, or otherwise potentially impactful for the NeurIPS community. Two choices: 2 This work is different enough from typical submissions to potentially have a major impact on a subset of the NeurIPS community. 1 This work is incremental and unlikely to have much impact even though it may be technically correct and well executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an opportunity to flag high-potential papers independent of technical quality; impact may diverge from quality (e.g., technically strong but unlikely to generate follow-up research, or flawed but likely to open new directions). Use impact to highlight novelty or potential community influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence Score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give a confidence score between 1 and 5 for each paper. Interpretations: 5 The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature. 4 The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain; unlikely but conceivable the reviewer missed something. 3 The reviewer is fairly confident; possible the reviewer did not understand parts or missed literature; mathematics/details not carefully checked. 2 The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely they did not understand central parts. 1 The reviewer’s evaluation is an educated guess (paper not in area or extremely difficult to understand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide honest confidence to help PC weight evaluations; confidence helps interpret the quantitative and qualitative assessments during deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper technically sound? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results? Is this a complete piece of work, or merely a position paper? Are the authors careful (and honest) about evaluating both the strengths and weaknesses of the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on technical correctness, sufficiency of evidence, completeness of the contribution, and author rigor/honesty. Quality is a core component reviewers are asked to address in free-text review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper clearly written? Is it well-organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? (A superbly written paper provides enough information for the expert reader to reproduce its results.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make suggestions to improve manuscript organization and readability where applicable. Clarity also relates to reviewer confidence and may correlate with future citation impact; reviewers should assess reproducibility of results and sufficiency of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the problems or approaches new? Is this a novel combination of familiar techniques? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions? Is related work adequately referenced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check recent NeurIPS proceedings to make sure the paper is sufficiently different from prior work; explicitly state how the submission departs from or extends existing contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results important? Are other people (practitioners or researchers) likely to use these ideas or build on them? Does the paper address a difficult problem in a better way than previous research? Does it advance the state of the art in a demonstrable way? Does it provide unique data, unique conclusions on existing data, or a unique theoretical or pragmatic approach?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge likely impact on the field, applicability, and whether the work advances state-of-the-art; support your assessment with concrete reasons or evidence in the review text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload limit to keep review quality high
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep quality of reviews high, reviewers were not assigned more than 5 papers; most reviewers received 4 papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain low reviewing load per reviewer to improve review quality and thoroughness; program committees should consider limiting assignments as a procedural quality control measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scores should reflect absolute judgments (do not normalize across assigned set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should NOT assume that they have received an unbiased sample of papers, nor should they adjust their scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not perform post-hoc normalization of scores to fit a desired distribution; base scores on each paper's merits relative to the community standards described in the numeric mapping and qualitative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Calibration (address differing interpretations of scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibration of reviewers is the process where different interpretations of the reviewing scale are addressed. Previous models used include Platt & Burges (2006) and a Bayesian variant by Welling & Ghahramani (2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibration can be modeled statistically (e.g., treat reviewer offsets and subjective noise, estimate objective paper quality and reviewer bias parameters). Programs may apply calibration algorithms (e.g., Bayesian models) at decision time to reduce inter-reviewer inconsistency and better estimate underlying paper quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: separate component scores (clarity, rigour, significance, originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion that scores could be separated out to improve consistency between reviewers; for example reviewers could be asked to score across clarity, rigour, significance and originality rather than a single aggregate quality score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rankings could then be determined through some combination of these component scores agreed at the program committee level, reducing variability caused by different reviewers weighting underlying factors differently.
